intro: The Torah, the first five books of the Tanakh, begins with two long books that most readers know at least in pieces: Genesis (Bereshit) and Exodus (Shemot). Genesis moves from the creation of the world to one family and its promises. Exodus follows that family, now a people, out of slavery, to a mountain, and into the building of a tent for God to dwell among them. Together they set up nearly everything the rest of the Tanakh assumes.

In this unit you will read these books the way Jewish tradition reads them, as Torah studied week by week, and the way historians and literary readers read them, as texts from the ancient Near East with a shape, a style and a history. You will meet Rashi and the midrash, the Epic of Gilgamesh and the Code of Hammurabi, the Passover Haggadah and the spiritual "Go Down, Moses." You will not be asked to decide whether the stories are true; you will be asked to say what they say and how their readers have read them.

By the end you will be able to name the parts of Genesis and Exodus in order, explain key terms such as covenant, parashah, Akedah, Aseret HaDibrot and Mishkan, quote passages in the JPS 1917 translation, compare a biblical story with a neighboring ancient text, and describe how the same verses are read differently by Jewish and Christian readers and by historians.
bigQuestion: How do Genesis and Exodus turn the story of a world, a family and a rescue into the covenant that the rest of the Tanakh builds on?

timeline.t: The Code of Hammurabi is written in Babylon; its case laws are later compared with the Torah's
Ramesses II begins his reign in Egypt and builds a city named Raamses
The Merneptah Stele names "Israel" as a people in Canaan, the oldest such mention
The Gilgamesh flood tablet is copied for the library at Nineveh
Most scholars place the writing down of Genesis and Exodus in this span, in stages (BCE)
The oldest surviving fragments of Genesis and Exodus, among the Dead Sea Scrolls
The Mishnah is edited; Pesachim 10 gives the earliest rules for the Seder
The Masoretic manuscripts fix the Hebrew text with vowels and notes
Rashi writes the commentary on the Torah that Jewish readers still study
"Go Down, Moses" is first printed after being heard at Fort Monroe, Virginia
George Smith reads the Gilgamesh flood tablet at the British Museum
The Jewish Publication Society publishes its English Tanakh, the translation this course quotes

words.d: "in the beginning"; the Hebrew name of Genesis, from its first word
"names"; the Hebrew name of Exodus, from its first words
a binding agreement; in the Torah, the bond between God and Israel, marked by a sign
one weekly portion of the Torah read in the synagogue
a rabbinic way of reading that fills gaps in the text with stories or teachings
"binding"; the story of the binding of Isaac in Genesis 22, read on Rosh Hashanah
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105), the most studied Jewish commentator on the Torah
Passover, the spring festival marking the leaving of Egypt; the story is retold at the Seder
"the telling"; the book that gives the order and words of the Passover Seder
the Ten Sayings; the Jewish name and count for the words spoken at Sinai in Exodus 20
"dwelling place"; the portable tent sanctuary described in Exodus 25–31 and 35–40
an Egyptian stone from c. 1208 BCE, the oldest object outside the Bible to name Israel

test.q: Which of these is the Hebrew name of the book of Genesis?
test.why: Bereshit, "in the beginning," is the first word and the Hebrew name of Genesis; Shemot is Exodus.

test.q: What do Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 have in common, according to the unit?
choices: Both name the woman Eve first
Both tell of creation, but in different orders and styles
test.why: The two accounts both describe creation, but the order of plants, animals and people differs, and so does the style.

test.q: What is the Epic of Gilgamesh compared with in this unit?
test.why: Tablet XI of Gilgamesh tells a flood story that scholars set beside Genesis 6–9.

test.q: Which story comes from midrash rather than from the text of Genesis?
choices: Hagar naming God at a spring
test.why: The idol story is in Genesis Rabbah; the other three are in Genesis 16, 32 and 41.

test.q: On which holiday is the Akedah, Genesis 22, read in the synagogue?
test.why: Genesis 22 is the reading for the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and the shofar recalls the ram.

test.q: What does the name Israel, given to Jacob, mean according to Genesis 32?
test.why: Genesis 32 explains the name as striving with God; Beth-El means house of God.

test.q: What is the climax of the Joseph novella?
choices: Joseph reveals himself to his brothers
test.why: The recognition scene in Genesis 45 is the moment the long single plot builds toward.

test.q: What can archaeology say about Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?
choices: It has proven they never lived
It can describe their world but no find names them either way
It shows they lived in Chicago
test.why: Digs reveal the cities and customs of the region, but no inscription names the ancestors.

test.q: How does Exodus 2 explain the name Moses?
choices: He was born in a basket
He was drawn out of the water
test.why: Exodus 2:10 links the name to a Hebrew verb for drawing out, because Pharaoh's daughter drew him from the water.

test.q: What do Jews say in place of God's four-letter name when reading Torah?
test.why: Tradition does not pronounce the name; Adonai, "my Lord," is read instead, and JPS 1917 prints "the LORD."

test.q: Which of these Seder practices comes from the Torah itself?
test.why: Exodus 12 commands unleavened bread; the cups, drops and leaning come from rabbinic and later custom.

test.q: In the Jewish count, what is the first of the Ten Sayings?
choices: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of Egypt
test.why: Jewish tradition counts the statement in Exodus 20:2 as the first saying; some Christian traditions call it an introduction.

test.q: How does rabbinic tradition read "eye for eye" in Exodus 21?
choices: As a law only for Egyptians
As a story, not a law
test.why: The Talmud's Bava Kamma reads the phrase as compensation, and Jewish law has followed that reading.

test.q: Why do many readers connect the Mishkan chapters to the creation story?
choices: Both are done in stages and end with blessing and rest
Both are sung at the Seder
test.why: Commentators note the Torah describes finishing creation and finishing the Mishkan in similar stages and words.

test.q: Why did enslaved African Americans sing "Go Down, Moses"?
choices: Because they saw their own bondage and hope in the Exodus story
Because the song was required by slaveholders
Because it was the Egyptian national song
test.why: In the spirituals, Egypt stood for the South and Pharaoh for the master; the Exodus story became their own story of freedom.

write.prompt: Does the Torah want its readers to remember slavery or to forget it? Argue from the text. Cite at least two of these: Exodus 20:2, Exodus 22:20 (JPS numbering) or 23:9, Deuteronomy 5:15, Exodus 13:8. Explain what each passage says and how at least one reader (Rashi, the Mishnah, the Haggadah, or the singers of "Go Down, Moses") has read it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you use.
Attribute every reading: "Rashi reads…", "the Haggadah says…", "the singers took…"; never "we believe."
Compare readings instead of ranking them; show what each reader saw in the words.
Use the unit's terms: covenant, Aseret HaDibrot, Seder, Haggadah, midrash.
Keep facts and readings apart: what the text says is one thing, what a reader makes of it is another.
